section_summary: This section contains 1946 correspondence about Japanese chemicals, glutamic acid, ceramics, sewing machines, cultured pearls, phonograph records, and fertilizer shortages, plus a 1948 letter about aluminum production. A substantial preliminary occupation report examines Japan’s fertilizer industry, imports, consumption, distribution, and requirements for 1946; the report continues beyond page 65.

subfiles.title: Reply concerning a report on the Japanese chemical industry
subfiles.about: Martin says the State Department has no public report on Japan’s chemical industry and suggests asking the War Department.
subfiles.summary: Martin directs Burke to the War Department’s Civil Affairs Division.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about recovery of Japanese chemical plants
subfiles.about: Burke asks where he can obtain an occupation report on the recovery of Japanese chemical plants.
subfiles.summary: Burke cites a Journal of Commerce article about a report prepared for Ambassador Pauley.

subfiles.title: Fertilizer requirements and shipment priorities for Japan
subfiles.from: Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers, Tokyo
subfiles.to: Secretary of State and U.S. military authorities
subfiles.about: Occupation authorities urgently request fertilizer and phosphate rock shipments to avert crop losses and food related unrest.
subfiles.summary: The telegram describes depleted soils, collapsing fertilizer production, and expected crop losses without imports. It gives historical production and import figures, requests delivery before July 1946, and warns that South Pacific phosphate supplies face mining and transport obstacles. Page 6 repeats much of page 5 in the supplied text.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about glutamic acid plants and production
subfiles.about: Darby asks about damage to Japanese glutamic acid plants and current or prospective production.
subfiles.summary: He identifies Suzuki Chemical Company as a former patent holder and mentions a possible name change to Rising Sun Company.

subfiles.title: Request for transport assistance for cultured pearl inspection
subfiles.about: The consulate asks whether to help Ernest S. Heller and Joseph Kolberg travel to Japan to inspect cultured pearls.
subfiles.summary: Heller seeks Army transport for a visit concerning pearl stocks and suitability for the American market.

subfiles.title: Instructions against assisting Heller’s Japan visit
subfiles.from: Dean Acheson, Acting Secretary of State
subfiles.about: The Department instructs the consul to provide no transport or other assistance for Heller or Kolberg’s Japan visit.
subfiles.summary: War Department and commercial officials had declined to sponsor the proposed trip.

subfiles.title: Congressional request for investigation
subfiles.about: A representative forwards constituent correspondence and requests facts for a reply.
subfiles.summary: The cover asks the Department to investigate and return the enclosed correspondence.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Darby’s glutamic acid inquiry
subfiles.about: Martin says occupation headquarters in Tokyo is being asked about glutamic acid production and export availability.
subfiles.summary: He promises to notify Darby when information arrives.

subfiles.title: Return of Darby correspondence
subfiles.about: Commerce returns Darby’s letter so State can clarify the purpose of his production inquiry.
subfiles.summary: Byse seeks the basis for requesting Japanese glutamic acid statistics.

subfiles.title: Foreign Economic Administration referral
subfiles.about: A form routes attached correspondence for action.
subfiles.summary: Routing form with handwritten remarks.

subfiles.title: Copy of Darby’s glutamic acid inquiry
subfiles.about: Darby requests information on damage to glutamic acid plants and expected Japanese production.
subfiles.summary: Copy of the letter on page 8.

subfiles.title: Request for justification of glutamic acid statistics inquiry
subfiles.about: Whitman asks Darby to explain the intended use and economic importance of the requested Japanese production data.
subfiles.summary: Occupation authorities lack capacity to investigate commodities unless their importance is established.

subfiles.title: Reply on recruitment of ceramic engineers
subfiles.about: The Department explains that the War Department sought ceramic engineers but General MacArthur withdrew the request.
subfiles.summary: The letter answers a constituent complaint and returns the enclosure.

subfiles.title: Objection to ceramic engineer recruitment for Japan
subfiles.about: Wendt urges Springer to stop recruitment of American ceramic expertise for Japan.
subfiles.summary: The pottery manufacturer argues that prewar Japanese dinnerware competition damaged his business and objects to public funding for technical advisers.

subfiles.title: Recruitment of ceramic engineers for military government
subfiles.about: Brewer seeks candidates for two ceramic engineering adviser posts in Japan.
subfiles.summary: The letter describes duties, salary, assignment length, transport, and living arrangements.

subfiles.title: Inquiry about Singer sewing machines and South American trade
subfiles.about: Bushfield asks State to investigate claims linking Japanese sewing machines to U.S. trade with South America.
subfiles.summary: He quotes a constituent alleging Japanese parts and machines displaced American work and that reciprocal food imports harmed farmers.

subfiles.title: Substantive reply to Bushfield on sewing machines and food imports
subfiles.about: State examines and largely rejects claims about Japanese Singer copies and South American grain and meat imports.
subfiles.summary: The reply distinguishes Japanese copies from Singer company production and finds no evidence that Japanese parts were assembled in the United States. It also disputes the alleged food trade arrangement, citing negligible grain imports, meat import restrictions, and limited price effects.

subfiles.title: Acknowledgment of Bushfield’s trade inquiry
subfiles.about: Byrnes acknowledges the sewing machine and South American trade inquiry and promises a fuller answer.
subfiles.summary: An interim acknowledgment of Bushfield’s May 28 letter.

subfiles.title: Routing slip for Tokyo despatch No. 508
subfiles.about: A routing slip identifies the Tokyo despatch that follows.
subfiles.summary: Internal routing for despatch No. 508.

subfiles.title: Reproduction of Japanese phonograph records in Brazil
subfiles.from: United States Political Adviser for Japan
subfiles.about: The political adviser forwards censorship comments on Japanese record matrices held by RCA of Brazil.
subfiles.summary: Despatch No. 508 encloses a G-2 letter and a report on records; the report is not present in this section.

subfiles.title: G-2 comments on Japanese phonograph records
subfiles.from: G-2, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: G-2 explains the status and limits of censorship comments on RCA of Brazil’s Japanese records.
subfiles.summary: Judgments based on remembered lyrics are informal unless a record was submitted for censorship.

subfiles.title: Army response on aluminum production proposals in Japan
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of the Army
subfiles.about: The Army reports on private proposals to process alumina in Japan and obtain aluminum and steel products.
subfiles.summary: SCAP had not submitted a proposal. The Army discusses the delicate reparations question and says contracts should not delay removal of capacity selected for reparations.

subfiles.title: Employment in inorganic nitrogenous fertilizer industries
subfiles.about: A table reports September 1946 employment in ammonium sulphate and calcium cyanamide industries.
subfiles.summary: Reports 76,207 employees in total.

subfiles.title: Population and labor force in Japan
subfiles.about: A census table divides Japanese population and labor force by sex and farm status.
subfiles.summary: Reports a population of 73.11 million.

subfiles.title: Value of inorganic nitrogenous fertilizer production
subfiles.about: A table compares fertilizer industry output value with total industrial production, 1932–1941.
subfiles.summary: Tracks ammonium sulphate and calcium cyanamide values.

subfiles.title: Consumption of inorganic nitrogenous fertilizer
subfiles.about: A table gives Japanese consumption of ammonium sulphate, calcium cyanamide, and sodium nitrate, 1926–1945.
subfiles.summary: Includes annual figures and period averages.

subfiles.title: Production of inorganic nitrogenous fertilizers
subfiles.about: A table records Japanese ammonium sulphate and calcium cyanamide production, 1926–1945.
subfiles.summary: Shows a steep fall in 1945.

subfiles.title: Subsidies paid to nitrogenous fertilizer manufacturers
subfiles.about: A table lists government subsidies per ton for ammonium sulphate and calcium cyanamide, 1940–1945.
subfiles.summary: Subsidies rose sharply during the war.

subfiles.title: Producers’ prices for inorganic nitrogenous fertilizers
subfiles.about: A table lists historical producer prices for ammonium sulphate and calcium cyanamide through 1946.
subfiles.summary: It notes government price setting from 1940.

subfiles.title: Fertilizers in Japan: A Preliminary Report, No. 55
subfiles.from: Natural Resources Section, Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers
subfiles.about: A preliminary report assesses Japan’s fertilizer supplies, industry, trade, consumption, crop needs, and 1946 outlook.
subfiles.summary: The report documents a collapse in commercial fertilizer use by 1945 amid import losses, factory damage, and scarce raw materials. It reviews field experiments, factory capacity, organic manures, imports and exports, price controls, and distribution. It recommends large 1946 supplies of nitrogenous, phosphatic, and potassic fertilizers, especially phosphate rock imports, to support food production. The report continues after page 65.
